paragraph1.content1: The number of officially recognized political prisoners in Belarus currently reaches more than

homePage.paragraph2: Each and every one of us has the opportunity to speak out against injustice through solidarity and this collective creative process

paragraph3.content2: is to tell about each illegally convicted citizen of Belarus and create their portraits using the traditional Belarussian technique of embroidery with red thread on a white background, and thus to record an important era of Belarusian history with a folk code ornament.

homePage.paragraph4: The process of embroidery is a long and meditative experience, allowing participants to concentrate on their thoughts and feelings for a particular arrestee. Time is what is taken away from a person in prison and time is the little we can sacrifice when creating a portrait of the political prisoner.

paragraph5.content: is a gesture of creative solidarity, allowing us to symbolically support people affected by the regime and share a story about their experience using a non-traditional tool of political protest - cross-stitching.

paragraph6.highlight: The final form of the project
paragraph6.content: will be a collective canvas of all the embroidered portraits and will be a material symbol of the intertwining of political events and human destinies.

section.title: Stitchit and Collective
section.paragraph1: Stitchit is an art group created in 2021 by visual artist Rufina Bazlova (Belarus) and curator Sofia Tocar (Moldova). The group works on burning socio-political issues using the traditional technique of embroidery as a tool of resistance and dialogue. Stitchit involves different communities and individuals into the creation process and blurs the lines of authorship.
section.paragraph2: Collective means all people, who take part in a project and activities organized by Stitchit.

terms.title: How to participate
terms.paragraph1: On this site, after confirming the conditions, you will receive detailed instructions that will guide you from the preparation stage to sending us your finished work.
terms.paragraph2: By taking part in the project you become an "ambassador" of a prisoner and will receive a "portrait" of a political prisoner in Belarus. All stories are equally important in this project, and we would like to immortalize all of them, so each political prisoner is embroidered only once.

paragraph3.content2: however, children of all ages may participate in the project if enabled by a parent or legal guardian.

paragraph4.content1: The work process is divided into several steps that you can go through at your own pace. However, we have set a time limit of
paragraph4.content2: This should be enough if you do occasional embroidery on your free evenings (even if you're just a beginner).

paragraph5.highlight1: If you do not finish your work in 2 months
paragraph5.content1: and do not tell us you need more time, we may drop you from the project and pass your hero*ine to someone else. We regret these strict rules, but we need to create some boundaries so the project does not turn into chaos.

paragraph6.content1: If you decide to withdraw from the project for any reason, or
paragraph6.highlight1: if you will not be able to finish your embroidery
paragraph6.content2: work on time, please let us know as soon as possible.

terms.paragraph7: Your work becomes a donation to “Stitchit” that is running this project and it becomes its property. The association can exhibit it, use it publicly or otherwise as it sees fit for the purpose of this project.

paragraph8.content1: An important element of the project is the photo documentation of your embroidery process and final work. These
paragraph8.highlight1: photos will be later used on the website and in other publications on the project.
paragraph8.content2: Therefore, we want to warn you about it in advance and ask you to take the quality of future photos seriously.

terms.paragraph9: At the end, we will also ask you to write a short comment about your experience embroidering a political prisoner and participating in the project. Embroidery is a slow-paced process that allows you to gain a better experience and understanding of the story you will be working on. We would love to hear your thoughts, as they may become an addition to your work.
terms.paragraph10: Please be aware that this comment will be published in our web gallery and may be used in print and online publications, exhibitions, etc. in the context of project presentations.

section2.title: How big does my embroidery have to be?
section2.paragraph1: Choose any canvases that you feel most comfortable working with. The size of the embroidery will depend on that image. Each job will be a little different in format - that's ok, we take this into account.

section3.title: How much fabric do i buy?
section3.paragraph1: You can use any fabric with a cross weave, or buy a special fabric for embroidery - Aida. To accurately determine the size of the fabric, you need to count 145 cells on the canvas. However, counting so many cells is too long and complicated, so we suggest counting 10 cells, measuring the distance with a ruler and multiplying by 14,5. To the result add about 5 cm on each side - this will be your final size.
section3.paragraph2: The fabric for the embroidery is called Aida. It comes in a different raster - the number behind the word Aida determines how many crosses fit in one centimetre.
section3.paragraph3: The smaller the number - the larger the cross. Usually it is sold in metres of 140 cm width.
section3.paragraph4: We've calculated in advance how much Aida fabric you might need in different widths - see the size chart:

section5.title: And a hoop?
section5.paragraph1: You don't need a hoop for this type of embroidery, but if it makes you feel more comfortable, use one!

section6.title: How to embroider?
section6.paragraph1: We suggest that you start in the middle of your embroidery. Fold the fabric in half twice - this is how you will find the centre of the fabric. The centre is also marked on the diagram. This is your starting point. Count off the number of empty cells from the centre to the beginning of the motif - this is usually the foot of the schematic character. Do the same on the fabric.
section6.paragraph2: Continue the work, counting the empty and filled cells. Follow the scheme. The number of crosses is already counted in the most complicated places.

section7.title: Work signature
section7.paragraph1: Instead of the "YOUR NAME, CITY, YEAR" line, sign the final embroidery with your name or pseudonym. If you worked on the embroidery collectively, have everyone embroider their name/pseudonym. We enclose a Latin and Belarusian alphabet from which you will make up your signature. You can come up with your own font. It would be great if you could also embroider the place you are from, the date, or any other text. If you think your work should be accentuated by decorations, add them.
section7.paragraph2: Please don't be afraid to make mistakes - the embroidery does not have to be perfect, let it be ORIGINAL, be YOURSELF!

section3.title: Write a letter to your political prisoner

paragraph1.content: You can mail a letter from your country. The full list of political prisoners with updated addresses is provided

paragraph2.content2: can help you send a postcard or a letter "online". Volunteers will transcribe your text and send it by mail in Belarus. Volunteers will translate your message from English into Belarusian. When the response comes, they can translate it into English on your demand. You can find more information on how to support the initiative on their page.

section3.paragraph3: What do you need to know about writing letters to prisoners?

paragraph4.content: All letters go through censorship. Don‘t write anything that may cause harm to you, your addressee or other people. Remember, that some of the information might not pass through censorship, so describe news and events carefully.

paragraph5.content: Write the date on the letter. You can also give it a number – it helps to figure out which letters get lost and how much time is needed for delivery.

paragraph6.content: Not all censors speak English. Most prisons only accept letters in Russian or Belarusian. So use a translator or an initiative where volunteers will translate your letters. Letters with unknown abbreviations, word reductions and words may not go through censorship. Also, don‘t send poems or literary works in the letters – they have a low chance of passing censorship.

section1.paragraph1: This can be phases of the embroidery, you at work, travel or events where you "were" with the embroidered Hero*ine, etc.

paragraph3.highlight: Please be aware that these photos may be used in print and online publications, exhibitions, etc. in the context of project presentation.

step5Page.title: Comment

section1.title: Write a short comment about your experience of embroidering a political prisoner
section1.paragraph1: It could be interesting stories that happened to you in the context of the project or facts that you learned during this time about your hero, about Belarus, etc. It could be quotes from your correspondence with the political prisoner or your thoughts that arise during the work. Here you can also write wishes for your hero, his/her family, to all Belarusians or our project. This can take the form of an open letter.
section1.paragraph2: We would like to know if the project has left any resonance in you? Did participating in the project bring you any new experiences? Your answer will help us improve the project.
section1.paragraph3: It would be wonderful if you can also write a handwritten comment and send it to us together with the finished embroidery. Because the handwritten text looks better when installed on the exhibitions.
